title: API Design Cheat Sheet
subtitle: The conventions interviewers expect in five minutes of API design — and the small details that separate a good answer from a great one.
seoTitle: API Design Cheat Sheet for System Design Interviews
description: REST conventions, pagination, idempotency, async operations, auth and errors — the API details that come up in system design interviews.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: The API step is short, but it's where interviewers check that you think about the contract between client and server. Aim for one endpoint per functional requirement, then sprinkle in the details below where they matter.

rows: Plural resource nouns, verbs come from the HTTP method
Request body for data, path for identity
Return the created resource (or its id)

blocks.code:
❌ POST /users/{userId}/posts        (anyone can post as anyone)
✅ POST /posts                        Authorization: Bearer <token>

blocks.text: The server reads the user from the session or JWT. Putting `userId` in the path or body for the *current* user is the most common API mistake in interviews.

rows: Slow for deep pages; items shift when new ones arrive
Can't jump to an arbitrary page

blocks.text: **Default to cursor pagination** for anything that changes in real time. The cursor usually encodes the last item's sort key (e.g. `createdAt` + `id`).

The server stores the key with the result; a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of acting twice. Mention this for payments, orders, bookings — anything a double-click or timeout could duplicate. See [Payment Failure Scenarios](/learn/system-design/tips/payment-failure-scenarios).
Don't hold an HTTP request open for minutes.

blocks.code:
POST /exports            → 202 Accepted { jobId }
GET  /exports/{jobId}    → { status: "running" | "done", url? }

blocks.text: Then let the client poll, or push completion via WebSocket, server-sent events or a webhook.
Uploads and Downloads of Big Files
Large bytes go straight to object storage via pre-signed URLs; your servers only handle metadata. Chunked/multipart uploads let big files resume.

rows: Updates every few seconds are fine
OK / Created / OK with no body
Not found (also good for "not yours" to avoid leaking existence)
Conflict — seat already taken, version mismatch
Temporarily unavailable — safe to retry later

blocks.text: For "edit the same thing at the same time" problems, use optimistic concurrency:

blocks.code:
GET  /docs/42            → { …, version: 7 }
PUT  /docs/42            If-Match: 7   → 200, or 409 if someone saved version 8 first

rows: Default for public/client APIs — say this and move on
Many client types need different shapes of the same data
Internal service-to-service calls where performance matters

blocks.text: Don't spend more than one sentence on this unless the interviewer asks. "REST for the client API, gRPC between internal services" is a complete answer.
